blurb: Learning from reward: exploration, deep RL on Atari, AlphaGo, and RL leaving the lab.

cards.title: Trial and error

steps.p: An agent observes a situation, takes an action and receives a reward and a new situation.
The goal is not the next reward but the sum of rewards over time, which can mean sacrificing now for later.
Through many episodes, the agent learns which actions lead to the most reward in each situation.

cards.aside: No one tells the agent the right move — only, eventually, how well it did.

cards.q: The exploration-exploitation trade-off is about choosing between…
options: Trying new actions to learn more versus using the best action known so far
cards.why: Learn or earn. Always exploiting may miss better options; always exploring wastes reward. Good agents balance both, like trying a new restaurant occasionally.

cards.statement: In reinforcement learning, the agent is told the correct action at each step.
cards.why: False. That is supervised learning. An RL agent only gets reward signals, often delayed, and must work out which actions earned them.

cards.q: A discount factor of 0.99 means a reward 100 steps in the future is worth about what fraction of an immediate one?
cards.why: 0.99¹⁰⁰ ≈ 0.37. Discounting makes nearer rewards count more, keeps infinite sums finite, and encodes uncertainty about the far future.

cards.title: In 1992, a program called TD-Gammon taught itself backgammon to near world-champion level by playing against itself.
cards.detail: Gerald Tesauro's network learned from self-play using temporal-difference learning, and even changed how experts played some opening moves.

options: Who gets paid for the model
Which of many earlier actions deserve credit for a later reward
cards.why: Which move mattered? A chess win comes at the end; RL must figure out which moves along the way actually contributed.

cards.title: DQN

steps.p: DeepMind's Deep Q-Network took raw screen pixels and the score, and output the value of each joystick action.
It stored past moments in a memory and trained on random samples, breaking up correlated consecutive frames.
A slowly updated copy of the network provided training targets, preventing the learning from chasing itself.

cards.aside: Published in Nature in 2015, DQN helped make DeepMind famous and led to Google acquiring it.

cards.statement: DQN used the same architecture and settings across all 49 Atari games it was tested on.
cards.why: True. That generality was the point: one algorithm, no game-specific tuning, reaching human-level play on many games.

cards.q: Why does experience replay help training?
options: Sampling randomly from past experience breaks the strong correlation between consecutive frames
cards.why: Decorrelation. Training on consecutive frames is like studying one page over and over. Random replay gives more varied, stable updates.

cards.title: The original DQN scored zero on Montezuma's Revenge.
cards.detail: The game requires long sequences of precise moves before any reward appears. Random exploration almost never stumbled onto points, making it a famous benchmark for exploration research.

cards.statement: Sparse rewards make reinforcement learning easier.
cards.why: False. With rewards far apart, the agent gets almost no feedback. Researchers add curiosity bonuses, demonstrations or shaped rewards to help.

options: The expected total future reward of taking an action in a given state
cards.why: Expected future reward. If you know Q for every action, picking the highest is the optimal policy.

cards.title: Mastering Go

steps.p: Go has more possible positions than atoms in the observable universe, so brute-force search was hopeless.
AlphaGo used a policy network to suggest moves and a value network to judge positions, steering Monte Carlo tree search.
AlphaGo Zero then learned from scratch by playing itself, and surpassed the original within days.

cards.aside: In March 2016, AlphaGo beat world champion Lee Sedol 4–1 in Seoul.

cards.q: AlphaGo's famous Move 37 in game two was striking because…
options: Its own model estimated a human would play it about 1 in 10,000 times — yet it was strong
cards.why: Creative, not copied. Commentators first thought it was a mistake. It showed AlphaGo had found ideas beyond human practice.

cards.statement: AlphaGo Zero learned from databases of human games.
cards.why: False. "Zero" meant zero human data: it started from random play and learned only by playing itself, then beat the original AlphaGo 100–0.

cards.title: Lee Sedol won one game against AlphaGo, with a brilliant move later called "the divine move".
cards.detail: His Move 78 in game four confused AlphaGo. He retired in 2019, saying AI was "an entity that cannot be defeated".

options: Learning to plan without being told the game's rules
cards.why: Learning the rules. MuZero learned its own model of the environment's dynamics and planned with it, mastering Go, chess, shogi and Atari.

cards.q: What role did Monte Carlo tree search play in AlphaGo?
options: Looking ahead by simulating promising move sequences guided by the neural networks
cards.why: Guided look-ahead. The networks narrowed which moves to explore and how good positions were, so search focused on a tiny promising slice of the game tree.

cards.title: Leaving the game board

steps.p: Real-world trial and error is slow and risky, so agents usually train in simulators.
Policies that work in simulation often fail on real hardware because physics and sensors never match perfectly.
Varying friction, lighting and masses in simulation forces policies robust enough to survive reality.

cards.aside: RL's biggest real-world use today is arguably training language models.

cards.q: DeepMind's reinforcement learning system cut energy used for cooling Google's data centers by up to…
cards.why: About 40%, Google reported in 2016, by learning how to set cooling equipment based on sensor data.

cards.statement: OpenAI Five beat the reigning world champion team at Dota 2.
cards.why: True. In April 2019 it beat OG, then world champions, in a best-of-three — after training on the equivalent of thousands of years of games.

options: Varying simulation conditions widely so the learned policy copes with real-world differences
cards.why: Robustness through variety. If a policy works across thousands of simulated variations, the real world looks like just one more.

cards.title: OpenAI trained a robot hand to solve a Rubik's Cube using only simulated practice.
cards.detail: The 2019 project relied on heavy domain randomization. The hand still succeeded only part of the time on the hardest scrambles, showing how hard real dexterity is.

cards.title: Spot reward hacking at work
cards.body: People respond to rewards like RL agents: a team measured on tickets closed will close tickets, solved or not. Seeing the incentive explains the behavior.
cards.challenge: Name one metric at work or school that people optimize in a way that misses its real purpose.
